_what: Mutants that survive and that NO test can kill without lying about how the code is reached. Each entry names the code by its source TEXT rather than a line number, because line numbers drift and a stale entry must fail loudly rather than point at the wrong code. `mutants` is how many surviving mutants the entry accounts for; the ratchet subtracts it from the module's behavioural survivors to give `openGaps`, and a module is DONE when openGaps reaches zero. Adding a row here is a claim that must carry evidence — see `reason` and the section named in `source`.
_rules: An anchor must appear EXACTLY ONCE in its module, or the entry names the line too.
If the anchor no longer appears, the entry is STALE: re-triage it, do not edit the anchor to match.
Deleting the code is better than recording it here. Nine mutants left this ledger that way in 66ad43d8d.
This ledger may not be used to reach a threshold. It records what cannot be killed, not what we did not get to.

The service constructs its own AuthCacheManager, so no test can hand it one that lies. The pair is pinned from both directions (quick then full, full then quick, cleared, expired negative). entries.reason: The tally is read in exactly one place: the closing logger.info summary line. Skipping an increment, or flipping += to -=, changes three numbers inside that one sentence and nothing else — no file is written or left unwritten, no manifest saved or skipped, and the function returns void so no caller can read the count. Killing any of these five mutants would mean asserting the wording of the summary log line, which is the padding the ratchet exists to refuse.

entries.reason: Dropping the guard lets the loop read outcome.action on undefined, which throws a TypeError straight into the per-project catch immediately below. Either way the project contributes nothing to the tally, no file is written, and the sweep moves to the next project. entries.reason: Removing the null-manifest guard (or emptying its body) makes the very next line, project.aiFileHashes, throw a TypeError before any writer is constructed. Nothing reaches the disk on either path and the per-project catch in the caller keeps the sweep going in both, so the outcome for every observable collaborator — writer, configWriter, fs — is identical. entries.reason: This catch surrounds the best-effort save that runs after a refresh has already failed. Its body is a single logger.warn; emptying it swallows the save error exactly as the original does and then rethrows the ORIGINAL error on the next line either way. No test can see the difference without asserting the warn text, and the case needs a refresh failure, landed hashes, and a rejecting configWriter all at once.
entries.decision: none — a log-only catch body around an already-best-effort save

entries.reason: A removal can only come from writer.remove, and the only call sites are in skillsWriter, which runs inside refreshContextAndSkills — the tier-2 step the sweep runs only when stampStale is true. stampStale is itself the next operand of this same || chain, so report.removed.length > 0 can never be the sole reason moved is true, and dropping it changes no run the code can reach. The operand is kept because it stops the rule depending on where removals happen to live.

entries.reason: writeSkill is a closure called from exactly one place: a map over DEMO_BUILDER_SKILLS, whose names come from the DEMO_BUILDER_ALWAYS_ON_SKILLS const tuple in @/types/ai. Every name is a compile-time literal with no path separator, so path.basename(name) always equals name and the throw is unreachable for any input the program can construct. Reaching it means replacing that tuple, which changes what the module IS rather than what it does; the guard stays as defence in depth for a future name.
entries.decision: keep — a traversal guard on a set fixed at compile time

entries.reason: Stryker drops the trailing $ anchor. The group before it is [\s\S]* — greedy, matching every remaining character including newlines — so the anchor is satisfied at the same position whether or not it is written, for every possible input. The regex has no m flag, so $ cannot match anywhere but end of input either. The two patterns accept exactly the same strings and capture exactly the same groups.
entries.decision: keep — $ documents the intent; it constrains nothing a greedy tail has not already

entries.reason: readOrUndefined's catch body is a single 'return undefined'. Emptying the block makes control fall off the end of the function, which returns undefined as well — the two versions produce the identical value for the identical inputs, and the function has no other effect. There is no input, and no collaborator, that can tell them apart.
entries.decision: keep — the explicit return states the contract the fall-through would only imply

entries.reason: This catch wraps the .gitignore append, which is documented non-fatal: the function returns normally whether the append succeeded or failed, and nothing downstream reads a result. Its body is one getLogger().warn. Emptying it leaves the same return, the same absent .gitignore entries and the same state on disk — only the warn stops printing, and asserting log wording is the padding the ratchet refuses.
entries.decision: keep — the warn is the only way an SC learns the entries are missing

entries.reason: Stryker replaces the empty-array default with an array holding its own marker string. The value is used once, as selectedIds.includes(seed.id), so the two defaults differ only for a seed whose CATALOG ID is that exact marker string. Writing a test around a Stryker-inserted literal would assert on the mutation tool rather than on the component, and no real catalog entry can carry that id.
entries.decision: keep — the empty default is correct; the difference is unreachable for real catalog ids

entries.reason: Emptying this catch body changes nothing a test can observe. The contract is that ensureHomeAiContext never throws, and that is the catch itself, not its body; the body's only statement is a process.stderr.write. With the body gone the function still swallows the failure and still resolves undefined, and every file it did manage to write is still written. The only difference is whether a warning line reaches stderr, which is wording, and the tests already pin the never-throws half in 'never throws when a write fails'.
entries.decision: none — the warning is the right thing to emit on a best-effort path; there is nothing else to assert

entries.reason: Same shape as the ensureHomeAiContext catch: the body is an ENOENT early return plus one process.stderr.write, so emptying it leaves refreshHomeAgentsMd resolving undefined on every failure exactly as it does now. No file is written either way and no value is returned either way, so the only observable difference is whether a warning line reaches stderr. The never-throws contract is pinned by two tests already.
entries.decision: none — the catch is correct; its body is reporting only

entries.reason: This guard chooses between two ways of saying nothing. On the ENOENT arm it returns; on the other arm it writes one warning to stderr and then returns. Both arms resolve undefined, write no file and leave the previously written AGENTS.md in place, so forcing the condition true, forcing it false, flipping the equality, or emptying the return block all produce the same result for every caller. The only observable difference is whether a warning line prints, and the optional chain on the same line IS killed by a test (a rejection carrying no value must not throw).
entries.decision: none — a missing projects root is genuinely not worth reporting, and the guard is the only way to say that

entries.reason: Stryker replaces the empty-array default with its marker array ["Stryker was here"]. Both defaults answer the same question the same way for every id this predicate is ever asked about: a mesh catalog id is never the marker string, so includes() returns false either way when the selection is absent. The only input that would tell them apart is a mesh component whose catalog id is literally 'Stryker was here', which the catalog cannot produce and a test asserting it would be asserting the mutation testing tool rather than the wizard.
entries.decision: none — the ?? [] default is the correct guard for an absent selection list

entries.reason: Dropping this optional chain to eds.daLiveAuth can only throw when edsConfig is undefined, and this clause is never evaluated in that case: the preceding clause reads Boolean(eds?.githubAuth?.isAuthenticated), which is false for an undefined edsConfig and short-circuits the &&. entries.decision: none — the ?. is required by the optional type and unreachable-with-undefined by short-circuit

entries.reason: Forcing the recorded !== undefined guard true leaves provablyOursByHash as sha256(onDisk) === recorded, and sha256 always returns a 64-character hex string, which is never equal to undefined. So for an unrecorded file both the guarded and the unguarded form evaluate to false, and for a recorded file the guard was true anyway. No input distinguishes them; the guard is there to state the precondition to a reader, not to change the answer.
entries.decision: none — the explicit guard says what proof-by-hash requires and costs nothing

Every id the loop cannot resolve is dropped: no source record is keyed by it, components.find returns undefined, and the iteration hits continue. The marker id therefore adds no row and the result is identical to the empty fallback.

entries.reason: The ArrayDeclaration mutant replaces the empty default with a one-element array whose element is not a DemoPackage. The default is read only by statusForArea -> isIntegrationsComplete -> meshComponentForStack, which does packages.find(p => p.id === state.selectedPackage). A junk element has an undefined id, so it is selected ONLY when selectedPackage is undefined; and a non-package pkg resolves getResolvedMeshRequirement to undefined and nativeForPackages?.includes(undefined) to false, so every entry comes back 'optional' and the mesh?.requirement === 'required' branch is not taken - exactly the outcome of pkg being undefined. Probed directly: buildYourProjectAreas(state, stacks) and buildYourProjectAreas(state, stacks, junk) return byte-identical results across six state shapes (no stack, EDS stack, undefined package, real package id, deployable selected, commerce configured).
entries.decision: none - the default's only consumer cannot see a non-package element, so no input distinguishes [] from a junk-filled array.

That operand is reached only when the left side of the && already held, and the left side is Boolean(state.edsConfig?.githubAuth?.isAuthenticated) — false whenever edsConfig is undefined. So && short-circuits before the mutated access on exactly the input that would make it throw, and no state can reach it: edsConfig defined means the property access is safe, edsConfig undefined means the expression is never evaluated. The type still requires the '?.' because edsConfig is optional on WizardState.
entries.decision: none - the '?.' is required by the type and unreachable behind the && short-circuit.

entries.reason: Removing this empty-href guard changes nothing: an empty href fails every later test the same way. It does not start with the source base URL, the scheme regex and the '//' test both fail on an empty string, and the very next guard returns for anything not starting with '/'. Verified by re-running consider() over a 33-href corpus (empty, whitespace, root, anchors, relatives, schemes, absolute same-site and foreign URLs, media, product overlays, .html collapse) with the guard removed: identical output per href and in aggregate.

Whatever this guard would have returned for, that one refuses to add. Verified by re-running consider() over a 33-href corpus with the guard removed and with && substituted: identical output per href in both cases. The final guard is NOT equivalent in the same way - '/.html' collapses to '/' after the extension strip and only line 119 catches it - so it is killed by a test rather than recorded here.

The copy's outcome, the uploaded html and the patch report are all identical, and the report path - the branch that actually records something - is asserted by its own test.

Both arms then run the same statement and the function returns false either way, so no caller, no response and no written document differs. The only observable difference is which channel the line lands on.
entries.decision: none - the sole effect is log level; asserting it would pin the logger call rather than behaviour.

entries.reason: Emptying this inner try leaves errorDetail as the empty string it was initialised to, and errorDetail is read in exactly one place: the warn line that reports a failed copy. The function returns false either way, nothing is written, and the caller sees the same boolean. The try exists only so an unreadable response body cannot turn a reported failure into a thrown one, and that IS tested - a response whose text() rejects still returns false.
entries.decision: none - the block's only product is text inside a log line.

entries.reason: This is the return after the retry for-loop, and it is unreachable: every iteration either returns or hits the catch, and the catch's last attempt (attempt === MAX_RETRY_ATTEMPTS) returns false rather than continuing. TypeScript cannot see that the loop always exits by return, so it requires a terminal return here; deleting it does not compile. Stryker reports it as NoCoverage for the same reason no test can reach it.
entries.decision: none - required by the compiler, unreachable at runtime.

entries.reason: The mutant drops the path === '/' operand only. The very next operand, path.endsWith('/'), is true for '/' as well, so the disjunction still holds and the function still returns false without probing. There is no path for which the two disagree: every string equal to '/' ends with '/'. The other two operands of the same condition ARE tested - a .html path is never probed and a path whose .html is not at the end is.
entries.decision: none - the operand is fully subsumed by the endsWith('/') test beside it.

entries.reason: The mutant drops the status === 204 operand. 204 is inside the 2xx range, so Response.ok is true for it and the disjunction still holds - a real 204 still reports success. Distinguishing the two would need a Response with status 204 and ok false, which the platform does not produce; fabricating one in a fixture would assert against a shape that cannot occur. The 204 case itself is tested and passes through the ok operand.
entries.decision: none - 204 already satisfies response.ok; the explicit test is belt-and-braces.

The value is read once, by the ternary bodyText ? ` - ${...}` : '', and both '' and undefined are falsy, so the error string built from it is character-for-character the same. A test covers the unreadable-body case and asserts the exact message, which is identical under both.
entries.decision: none - both fallbacks are falsy and the only reader is a truthiness test.

The filtering itself has already happened on the line above and is asserted by tests (overlays dropped, the default template kept), so every mutant here - flipping the subtraction, forcing or dropping the guard, loosening the comparison, emptying the block - leaves the copied path list, the writes and the result identical.

Both index spellings are tested as excluded from the copy, so forcing the branch, dropping it, loosening the comparison or emptying the block changes nothing a caller can see - only whether one info line prints.

(Mutated together with the auth-page continue the two would differ; Stryker mutates one at a time, and each alone is invisible.)
